blocks.text: The anions (acid radicals) are identified by the following tests on the solid sample, each with its experiment, observation and inference.

Take about 2 g of the solid carbonate sample in a clean test tube and add about 5 cm3 of dilute HCl; pass the gas evolved through lime water. Effervescence takes place, a gas evolves briskly and it turns lime water milky: carbonate ions are indicated.

blocks.title: Carbonate test
blocks.text: CO3 2-(aq) + 2H+(aq) -> H2O(l) + CO2(g); Ca(OH)2(aq) + CO2(g) -> CaCO3(s) (white ppt) + H2O(l)
b) Chloride, bromide and iodide, Cl-, Br-, I-

Take 2 g of the solid sample in a test tube and add 5 cm3 of distilled water to make the aqueous solution. Add a few drops of dilute HNO3 to acidify the solution, then about 5 cm3 of aqueous AgNO3. A thick white precipitate that dissolves in aqueous NH3 indicates Cl-; a thick cream-yellow precipitate indicates Br-; a bright yellow precipitate indicates I- (Figure 16.7). The dilute nitric acid is added to prevent the precipitation of carbonate ions along with the halide ions.

blocks.title: Silver halides
blocks.text: Ag+(aq) + Cl-(aq) -> AgCl(s) white ppt; Ag+(aq) + Br-(aq) -> AgBr(s) cream-yellow ppt; Ag+(aq) + I-(aq) -> AgI(s) bright yellow ppt

blocks.alt: Three test tubes labelled A, B and C. A contains a white precipitate tagged CHLORIDE (WHITE), B a cream precipitate tagged BROMIDE (CREAM) and C a yellow precipitate tagged IODIDE (YELLOW).
blocks.caption: Figure 16.7: Observation of reactions of halide ions with AgNO3 (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 16.7).

blocks.text: Take 2 g of the solid sample in a clean test tube and dissolve it in 5 cm3 of distilled water. Add 5 cm3 of sodium hydroxide solution, then 3 g of powdered aluminium metal. A characteristic smell of ammonia gas is felt near the mouth of the test tube and the gas turns red litmus paper blue: nitrate ions are indicated. Aluminium metal reduces nitrate ions to ammonium ions, which react with the aqueous NaOH to evolve ammonia; the reduction of nitrate by aluminium is a redox reaction in which the aluminium acts as the reducing agent.

blocks.alt: A test tube of test solution held at an angle over a Bunsen burner, with a strip of litmus paper (red changing to blue) at its mouth. Tags: LITMUS PAPER, TEST SOLUTION, BUNSEN BURNER.
blocks.caption: Nitrate test (original drawing after the figure printed in the textbook).

blocks.text: Take 3 g of the solid sample in a clean test tube and dissolve it in 5 cm3 of distilled water. Acidify the solution with a few drops of dilute HNO3 and add 5 cm3 of barium nitrate solution. A heavy white precipitate of BaSO4 is formed: sulfate ions are indicated. The dilute nitric acid destroys any carbonate ions present as an impurity.
Distinguish carbonate from bicarbonate, describe the ring test for nitrate, and name some water-insoluble sulfates.
